summary:
Eco-Urban-Space (EUS) Climate Intelligence Platform
​Developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, EUS is a serverless spatial analytics engine designed to combat escalating climate pressures, water shortages, and soil degradation. The platform integrates real-time NASA Earth Observations (including SMAP soil moisture, MODIS NDVI, and GPM precipitation metrics) with localized soil profiles and agricultural priorities via an advanced LangGraph and LlamaIndex orchestration pipeline. By dynamically generating optimized, multi-season crop rotation blueprints and decarbonization pathways, EUS bridges the gap between complex remote sensing data and actionable farm-level decision-making. This solution is critical for enhancing long-term agricultural resilience, conserving scarce water resources, and securing sustainable food systems in vulnerable regions.
details:
Project overview

EOAgriTool is a web-based farm decision-support project designed for Egyptian farmers and agricultural businesses. It brings together tools for monitoring farms, climate, water, energy, soil and sustainability in a single dashboard. The project aims to help users identify environmental and operational risks, make better-informed management decisions, conserve water and soil, improve resilience to climate-related stress and reduce agriculture’s environmental footprint. These are intended benefits rather than outcomes that have already been measured or demonstrated by the repository.

The project’s recommendation engine converts farm and resource measurements into prioritised actions, including estimated savings and potential yield-related benefits. Its sample Nile Delta crop-rotation plan illustrates this approach by considering crop selection, irrigation requirements, soil health and risk mitigation together. Rather than treating each challenge separately, EOAgriTool attempts to provide farmers with a more complete view of the relationships between resources, production and sustainability.

Current implementation

The repository shows that several core components are already implemented. The Python backend contains a rule-based recommendation engine and an energy-bill parser, while the frontend provides dashboard pages, forms, charts and visual summaries. Users can submit information such as irrigation volume, rainfall deficit, soil pH, organic matter, energy consumption, carbon footprint and previous crop. The system then evaluates those values and returns prioritised farm-management guidance.

Some capabilities described in the project materials remain planned rather than operational. The roadmap identifies live satellite feeds, Internet of Things connectivity and predictive analytics as future work. The climate page currently displays hard-coded sample data, so references in the README to real-time alerts and integration with satellite, drone and sensor data should be understood as intended capabilities rather than confirmed live features.

Technology stack

EOAgriTool primarily uses Python for its backend, with HTML, CSS and JavaScript supporting the browser-based interface. JSON files are used for sample plans and other structured data. The main application runs on Quart, an asynchronous Python web framework, and uses Hypercorn as its server.

Notable dependencies include Quart-CORS, httpx, Azure OpenAI, Azure Identity and Chart.js. Optional integrations support Cosmos DB conversation history and Azure Functions tool calling. The project can be deployed through Docker, while the deployment documentation also describes an Azure App Service configuration. Git is used for version control.

The main web application does not require specialised hardware. A separate script, EOAgriToolstandaloneApp.py, can detect an NVIDIA GPU and use vLLM, but this is an optional capability and is not required to run the principal Quart application.

There is a documentation inconsistency concerning the backend stack. The README refers to Node.js, Express and MongoDB or PostgreSQL, but the current application entry point and dependency file show that the implemented backend uses Python and Quart. The roadmap also presents Node.js and MongoDB as future technologies, suggesting that the README includes planned architecture alongside the project’s present implementation.

Repository organisation

The project separates backend logic, shared frontend resources, tests and supporting documents into distinct directories:

backend/ Quart routes and backend services
recommend/ Rule-based farm recommendations and energy-bill parsing
assets/ Shared frontend JavaScript and CSS
tests/ Recommendation and bill-parser tests
Documents/ Project reports
*.html Dashboard, fields, climate, water, reports, and other pages
app.py Main Quart application entry point
requirements.txt Python dependencies
Dockerfile Container build and startup configuration

The browser pages share navigation and local application state through assets/app.js, while Chart.js renders the visualisations. The app.py entry point creates the Quart application using routes defined in backend/routes.py. These routes serve the user interface and expose endpoints for farm recommendations, energy-bill parsing, sustainability goals and optional AI chat and conversation-history functions.

Creativity and design considerations

The project’s principal creative feature is the way it combines Earth-observation ambitions with practical regenerative-agriculture guidance. Instead of concentrating exclusively on maps or crop monitoring, its recommendation rules connect multiple farm concerns. For example, high irrigation readings can trigger water-saving recommendations, while low organic matter combined with alkaline soil can lead to targeted soil-management guidance.

The sample crop-rotation plan follows the same integrated approach. It links crop sequencing with estimated irrigation demand, nitrogen fixation, soil-health objectives and risks such as salinisation. This makes the project more than a visual monitoring dashboard: it is intended to translate environmental and farm data into practical management decisions.

The repository does not contain a record of the team’s discussions, so it cannot establish precisely which options the collaborators considered or why particular design decisions were made. However, the code and documentation reflect several important factors. These include the Egyptian farming context and a Nile Delta example; irrigation, rainfall, heat, drought and water availability; soil pH, organic matter, texture, salinity and nutrient availability; crop type, planting date, previous crop and rotation; and environmental and economic considerations such as carbon footprint, energy cost and potential water savings.

The materials also show attention to usability and delivery. The interface uses dashboards and visual summaries to make information more accessible, and the application includes fallback behaviour when optional services are unavailable. Deployment, security, accessibility and performance improvements are also identified in the project documentation.

Running the application

The documented local setup requires Python 3.9 or later, with Python 3.12 recommended in the deployment guide. Azure OpenAI settings are required for AI-assisted functionality, while Cosmos DB is optional and is used for conversation history.

python3.12 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
cp .env.example .env
# Configure the required service settings in .env as needed
python app.py

The deployment guide and .env.example file provide the relevant configuration settings. After the virtual environment has been created and the dependencies installed, the required service values can be added to the .env file before starting the application through app.py.

Main writing changes: I converted the source notes and bullet points into connected, presentation-ready paragraphs; separated implemented features from planned capabilities; retained the caution about unmeasured outcomes; and made the stack inconsistency explicit without overstating what the repository proves.
